A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same M2D2 continual-pretraining study. All 25 pages of v1 and 23 pages of v2, including appendix text, equations, tables and figures, support comparison despite substantial rewriting and reorganization.

before.justification: V1 reports original GPT2 and RoBERTa pretraining and transfer experiments, GPT2 BIG-Bench evaluations, and ablations in Section 4 and Appendix 7.

after.justification: V2 retains original empirical results and adds Llama2-7B experiments, prediction-rank analyses and additional randomized training orders in Section 4 and Appendix A.

M1.justification: Sequential pretraining with the original language-modeling objective remains unchanged. Section 4.6 adds a diagnostic procedure that cleans and clusters sentences, extracts keywords and target words, and measures target-token prediction ranks. This adds an analysis component without changing the core training algorithm.

E1.justification: Both versions use the same 159 M2D2 domains and five BIG-Bench tasks. The new rank analysis selects material from the already covered cs.AI test corpus for token-prediction evaluation. Llama2-7B and additional training orders expand configurations and protocols rather than dataset or task coverage.

E2.justification: Corresponding comparisons retain zero-shot evaluation and standalone per-domain training. V1's fine-tuning baseline is renamed domain-adaptive pretraining in v2, without an established procedural change. Llama2-7B expands the evaluated model configurations; no additional competing continual-learning algorithm is introduced.

E3.justification: V2 replaces mean perplexity aggregation with medians, adds best-prior-checkpoint forgetting and prediction-rank evaluation, and introduces Llama2-7B experiments with downstream evaluation at L2 checkpoints. Section 3 also changes the reported learning-rate setting from 5e-5 to automatic selection. These are substantial protocol changes, although the PDFs do not establish which retained experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: V2 adds keyword-rank knowledge analysis, domain-size versus adaptation analysis, and robustness checks using two additional randomized curricula. V1's optimization/generalization traces across four example domains, Figures 8 and 17, are removed. The batch-size, data-balancing and reversed-portion ablations are retained.

E5.justification: V1 explicitly acknowledges using only one randomized order. V2 Section 4.7 reports repeating GPT2-M training with two further shuffles and provides their individual median CPT results. This adds limited repeated-run evidence, without confidence intervals, reported standard deviations or significance tests.

E6.justification: Summary values and transfer trends change under revised aggregation: GPT2-small random-order CPT is 21.04 in v1 Table 2 versus 19.67 in v2 Figure 3, a mean-to-median replacement rather than a same-setting performance gain. V2 adds substantial Llama2-7B results, including worse CPT than zero-shot perplexity, downstream deterioration and worsening prediction ranks.

T1.justification: V1's mean-based metric definitions are replaced by median-based definitions, and v2 formally defines forgetting relative to the best previous perplexity. These revise the mathematical evaluation definitions; neither version develops a theorem or proof contribution.

C1.justification: V1 emphasizes CPT superiority over standalone adaptation when domains are semantically ordered. V2 claims superiority across orders and model families, while narrowing beneficial pretraining and downstream-performance claims to GPT2 and explicitly identifying Llama2-7B deterioration. Its headline scaling conclusions also more strongly assert better absolute performance and less forgetting for larger models.

C2.justification: V2 introduces explanations involving Llama2's much larger original training corpus, insufficient adaptation-domain size and impaired in-context performance. It qualifies the interpretation of Llama2's low forgetting scores because overall perplexity deteriorates. Limitations now address the single similar-order sequence and sequential computation costs, while the RoBERTa data-overlap caveat remains.

D1.justification: V2 adds approximate training durations of six days for GPT2-small and four months for Llama2-7B, plus preprocessing details for the rank-analysis pipeline. Conversely, replacing v1's explicit 5e-5 learning rate with unspecified automatic selection reduces hyperparameter specificity.

R1.justification: V2 extends the existing related-work discussion with multilingual adaptation, gradient localization, continual memorization and Geva et al.'s knowledge analysis. It adds contrasts with conventional vision CL benchmarks while retaining its central positioning as a long-horizon domain-pretraining benchmark. Cossu 2022 becoming Cossu 2024 is a publication update to the same work.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, findings and discussion are substantially rewritten. Results are reorganized into seven question-oriented subsections, limitations become a separate section, and the appendix reverses the RoBERTa/BIG-Bench discussion order. Terminology, model abbreviations and the author list also change.

P2.justification: V1 Tables 2, 4 and 5 become bar-chart displays in v2 Figures 3, 15 and 16. Transfer plots are substantially redrawn, including changed aggregation, improvement-axis direction and panel organization. The t-SNE figure moves into the main text; loss-trace figures disappear and new Llama2, rank and domain-size figures are introduced.

improvement.justification: V2 usefully establishes that GPT2's benefits do not extend to Llama2-7B and partially addresses v1's single-shuffle limitation. However, numerical consistency limits these gains: the extra-order analysis cites a 16.69 reference while Figure 3 reports 15.74 for random-order GPT2-M. The across-family adaptation-superiority claim also conflicts with RoBERTa-large in Figure 16, where similar-order CPT is 2.15 versus DAPT 1.58. The richer evidence improves applicability assessment, but these inconsistencies and less specific learning-rate reporting limit the net improvement.
